papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: Strategy Coopetition Explains the Emergence and Transience of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Why does in-context learning (ICL) emerge and then disappear (transience) during training, and what are the dynamics between ICL and other learning strategies?
papers.core_contribution: The transience of in-context learning (ICL) is explained by coopetition (cooperative and competitive dynamics) between ICL and a newly identified strategy called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), where shared sub-circuits enable ICL emergence before CIWL asymptotically dominates.
papers.conclusion: Strategy coopetition between ICL and CIWL explains the emergence and transience of ICL, providing a deeper mechanistic understanding of how capabilities dynamically trade off during transformer training.
papers.key_findings:
The asymptotic strategy after ICL transience is a hybrid called context-constrained in-weights learning (CIWL), which depends on both in-weights information and the presence of the correct label in context.
ICL and CIWL share critical sub-circuits (e.g., Layer 2 induction heads), leading to cooperative dynamics that enable ICL emergence.
ICL emergence is only possible when CIWL is not fully formed, and ICL is faster to emerge but asymptotically dominated by CIWL.
A minimal mathematical model captures the coopetition dynamics and explains transience.
Matching context and query exemplars in the data can make ICL persistent by removing the asymptotic bias towards CIWL.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a powerful ability that emerges in transformer models, enabling them to learn from context without weight updates. Recent work has established emergent ICL as a transient phenomenon that can sometimes disappear after long training times. In this work, we sought a mechanistic understanding of these transient dynamics. Firstly, we find that, after the disappearance of ICL, the asymptotic strategy is a remarkable hybrid between in-weights and in-context learning, which we term "context-constrained in-weights learning" (CIWL). CIWL is in competition with ICL, and eventually replaces it as the dominant strategy of the model (thus leading to ICL transience). However, we also find that the two competing strategies actually share sub-circuits, which gives rise to cooperative dynamics as well. For example, in our setup, ICL is unable to emerge quickly on its own, and can only be enabled through the simultaneous slow development of asymptotic CIWL. CIWL thus both cooperates and competes with ICL, a phenomenon we term "strategy coopetition." We propose a minimal mathematical model that reproduces these key dynamics and interactions. Informed by this model, we were able to identify a setup where ICL is truly emergent and persistent.

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: Explaining reaction coordinates of alanine dipeptide isomerization obtained from deep neural networks using Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
papers.research_question: How can Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods explain which collective variables contribute to the reaction coordinates predicted by deep neural networks for alanine dipeptide isomerization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that XAI methods (LIME and SHAP) can provide local explanations for the contribution of collective variables to reaction coordinates predicted by a deep neural network for alanine dipeptide isomerization, revealing the importance of specific dihedral angles.
papers.conclusion: The proposed AI-aided method combined with XAI provides a practical tool for locally explaining appropriate reaction coordinates from DNN training, especially near the transition state, and is applicable to complex molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks can be trained to predict appropriate reaction coordinates for alanine dipeptide isomerization.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide local explanations of feature contributions to the predicted reaction coordinates.
Near the transition state, the dihedral angle θ becomes more important than near the stable states, indicating its role in crossing the barrier.
The feature contributions from LIME and SHAP are consistent, justifying LIME's linear model assumption.
The method can identify dominant collective variables consistent with previous committor test analyses.
papers.limitation: Understanding the detailed mechanism for complex molecular systems becomes complicated because of the large numbers of collective variables.
future_direction: Application to solute-solvent systems such as alanine dipeptide in explicit water.
Application to various other solute-solvent systems.
papers.abstract: A method for obtaining appropriate reaction coordinates is required to identify transition states distinguishing the product and reactant in complex molecular systems. Recently, abundant research has been devoted to obtaining reaction coordinates using artificial neural networks from deep learning literature, where many collective variables are typically utilized in the input layer. However, it is difficult to explain the details of which collective variables contribute to the predicted reaction coordinates owing to the complexity of the nonlinear functions in deep neural networks. To overcome this limitation, we used Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods of the Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and the game theory-based framework known as Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). We demonstrated that XAI enables us to obtain the degree of contribution of each collective variable to reaction coordinates that is determined by nonlinear regressions with deep learning for the committor of the alanine dipeptide isomerization in vacuum. In particular, both LIME and SHAP provide important features to the predicted reaction coordinates, which are characterized by appropriate dihedral angles consistent with those previously reported from the committor test analysis. The present study offers an AI-aided framework to explain the appropriate reaction coordinates, which acquires considerable significance when the number of degrees of freedom increases.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning via Supportive Pretraining Data
papers.research_question: What makes certain pretraining data supportive for in-context learning, and what are the characteristics of such data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a gradient-based method (ORCA-ICL) to identify a small subset of pretraining data that supports in-context learning and analyzes the characteristics of this supportive data.
papers.conclusion: The work takes a first step towards understanding in-context learning by analyzing instance-level pretraining data, and the findings may guide future pretraining data construction to actively improve models' in-context learning performance.
papers.key_findings:
The supportive pretraining data for in-context learning do not have a higher domain relevance to downstream tasks compared to random pretraining data.
The supportive pretraining data contain a relatively higher mass of rarely occurring, long-tail tokens.
The supportive pretraining data are challenging examples where the information gain from incorporating long-range context is below average, indicating that learning to incorporate difficult long-range context encourages in-context learning.
A continued pretraining on the identified supportive subset significantly improves the model's in-context learning ability, by up to 18%, without improving zero-shot performance.
The cross-task effectiveness of the supportive data suggests that part of the in-context learning behavior is task-specific and not universal across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The supportive pretraining data are identified with respect to the current language model checkpoint, and early checkpoints might have different supportive data.
The ORCA-ICL method is computationally expensive due to its gradient-based nature and the large size of pretraining data.
future_direction: Convert the correlational findings to causal ones to actively refine or construct pretraining data for improved in-context learning.
Apply the ORCA-ICL method to generation tasks in addition to classification tasks.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) improves language models' performance on a variety of NLP tasks by simply demonstrating a handful of examples at inference time. It is not well understood why ICL ability emerges, as the model has never been specifically trained on such demonstrations. Unlike prior work that explores implicit mechanisms behind ICL, we study ICL via investigating the pretraining data. Specifically, we first adapt an iterative, gradient-based approach to find a small subset of pretraining data that supports ICL. We observe that a continued pretraining on this small subset significantly improves the model's ICL ability, by up to 18%. We then compare the supportive subset constrastively with random subsets of pretraining data and discover: (1) The supportive pretraining data to ICL do not have a higher domain relevance to downstream tasks. (2) The supportive pretraining data have a higher mass of rarely occurring, long-tail tokens. (3) The supportive pretraining data are challenging examples where the information gain from long-range context is below average, indicating learning to incorporate difficult long-range context encourages ICL. Our work takes a first step towards understanding ICL via analyzing instance-level pretraining data. Our insights have a potential to enhance the ICL ability of language models by actively guiding the construction of pretraining data in the future.

papers.title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: To what extent does a proxy-based, artificial decomposition of neuron activations (e.g., via sparse autoencoders) empirically benefit model interpretation compared to the organic features already represented within the original model's feed-forward layers?
papers.core_contribution: Features from feed-forward key-value memories (FF-KV) are nearly as interpretable as those from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and in some aspects (e.g., absorption, explained variance) even outperform SAEs, suggesting that FF-KV features serve as a strong baseline for interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Proxy-based methods such as SAEs offer very limited empirical advantage over direct analysis of feed-forward layers, and FF-KV features should be included as a strong baseline in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FF-KV features achieve comparable interpretability to SAE features across multiple automatic evaluation metrics from SAEBENCH.
FF-KV features sometimes outperform SAEs, e.g., in absorption (less redundancy) and explained variance (perfect by definition).
Human evaluation shows conceptual features can be found with almost equal ease from both FF-KV and SAEs.
Features discovered by proxy methods (e.g., Transcoders) often do not align with features in the original FF module, suggesting potential hallucination.
Increasing sparsity in FF-KV (via TopK) does not consistently improve interpretability across metrics.
papers.limitation:
SCR and TPP scores are highly unstable and should be treated as supplementary results.
The theoretical advantage of SAEs is not observed empirically through the current evaluation scheme.
future_direction: Further research on the faithfulness of learned features from proxy modules, with FF-KV features as grounding points.
Inclusion of FF-KV features as a baseline when assessing feature-discovery methods in interpretability.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability work on large language models (LLMs) has been increasingly dominated by a feature-discovery approach with the help of proxy modules. Then, the quality of features learned by, e.g., sparse auto-encoders (SAEs), is evaluated. This paradigm naturally raises a critical question: do such learned features have better properties than those already represented within the original model parameters, and unfortunately, only a few studies have made such comparisons systematically so far. In this work, we revisit the interpretability of feature vectors stored in feed-forward (FF) layers, given the perspective of FF as key-value memories, with modern interpretability benchmarks. Our extensive evaluation revealed that SAE and FFs exhibits a similar range of interpretability, although SAEs displayed an observable but minimal improvement in some aspects. Furthermore, in certain aspects, surprisingly, even vanilla FFs yielded better interpretability than the SAEs, and features discovered in SAEs and FFs diverged. These bring questions about the advantage of SAEs from both perspectives of feature quality and faithfulness, compared to directly interpreting FF feature vectors, and FF key-value parameters serve as a strong baseline in modern interpretability research.

papers.title: Quiet Feature Learning in Algorithmic Tasks
papers.research_question: Do Transformer-based models learn meaningful internal representations (quiet features) before showing improvement in task loss, and are these features causally necessary for performance?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer-based models learn 'quiet features' (intermediate algorithmic computations) during a slow phase where task loss is stagnant, and these features are causally necessary for the subsequent sharp drop in loss.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based models encode important intermediate computations well before they show significant gains in next-token prediction, revealing a gap between internal representation learning and external task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Phase transitions occur during learning: validation loss shows a slow phase with minimal improvement followed by a fast phase of rapid decrease.
Quiet features, representing intermediate algorithmic computations, are learned during the slow phase before any decrease in task loss.
Ablation experiments show that quiet features are causally necessary for task performance.
Feature learning curves can exhibit a U-shape, where probing loss for some quiet features increases after the phase transition, suggesting representation changes.
Phase transitions are observed across different compute budgets, model sizes, dataset sizes, and within individual training runs.
future_direction: Developing theoretical frameworks to explain why models accumulate latent subroutines before observable metric improvements.
Extending the analysis to larger, more complex models and natural-language settings.
Motivating new methods for probing and monitoring internal learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: We train Transformer-based language models on ten foundational algorithmic tasks and observe pronounced phase transitions in their loss curves that deviate from established power-law scaling trends. Over large ranges of compute, the validation loss barely improves, then abruptly decreases. Probing the models' internal representations reveals that quiet features are learned prior to any decrease in task loss. These quiet features represent intermediate algorithmic computations that do not by themselves improve the output loss. Ablation experiments demonstrate that individual quiet features are causally necessary for task performance. Our results demonstrate that substantial representational progress can remain hidden beneath an apparently flat loss curve, challenging the prevailing use of cross-entropy as a proxy for learning and motivating richer diagnostics for monitoring model training.

papers.title: Illusion or Algorithm? Investigating Memorization, Emergence, and Symbolic Processing in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the extent to which in-context learning (ICL) in language models reflects true generalization versus memorization, and how ICL abilities and mechanisms develop during pre-training.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that in-context learning (ICL) is not purely memorization nor purely symbolic algorithmic processing, and reveals predictable development patterns for complex ICL tasks linked to internal subspace allocation in the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that ICL is a mix of generalization and memorization, with predictable development for complex tasks, and internal mechanistic analysis reveals consistent subspace allocation patterns that advance understanding of ICL.
papers.key_findings:
LMs can perform pattern-based ICL tasks with random tokens, indicating generalization beyond memorization, but performance declines with rarer tokens, contradicting a pure symbolic algorithm view.
Different aspects of ICL develop idiosyncratically with model scale and training time, with performance gaps due to task configuration persisting while token frequency gaps stabilize.
The dimensionality of the residual stream subspace used for ICL follows a consistent pattern: an initial rise then decay, and development correlates with using a common subspace across tasks.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited by the availability of fine-grained checkpoints, particularly between steps 512 and 1000 in Pythia training, which could provide further insights.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more fine-grained checkpoint intervals.
Applying the SUDA method to a wider range of tasks in interpretability.
Systematic investigation across diverse factual and reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large-scale Transformer language models (LMs) trained solely on next-token prediction with web-scale data can solve a wide range of tasks after seeing just a few examples. The mechanism behind this capability, known as in-context learning (ICL), remains both controversial and poorly understood. Some studies argue that it is merely the result of memorizing vast amounts of data, while others contend that it reflects a fundamental, symbolic algorithmic development in LMs. In this work, we introduce a suite of investigative tasks and a novel method to systematically investigate ICL by leveraging the full Pythia scaling suite, including interim checkpoints that capture progressively larger amount of training data. By carefully exploring ICL performance on downstream tasks and simultaneously conducting a mechanistic analysis of the residual stream's subspace, we demonstrate that ICL extends beyond mere "memorization" of the training corpus, yet does not amount to the implementation of an independent symbolic algorithm. Our results also clarify several aspects of ICL, including the influence of training dynamics, model capabilities, and elements of mechanistic interpretability. Overall, our work advances the understanding of ICL and its implications, offering model developers insights into potential improvements and providing AI security practitioners with a basis for more informed guidelines.

papers.title: Cognitive Dissonance: Why Do Language Model Outputs Disagree with Internal Representations of Truthfulness?
papers.research_question: Why do language model outputs disagree with internal representations of truthfulness, and is this due to deception or other factors like confabulation and heterogeneity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that most disagreements between LM outputs and internal truthfulness representations are due to confabulation and heterogeneity, with deception being rare, and that probes are better calibrated than queries.
papers.conclusion: Disagreements between internal and external representations of truthfulness are predominantly due to different prediction pathways rather than latent deceptive intent, and the proposed taxonomy helps categorize these mismatches.
papers.key_findings:
Probes are consistently more accurate than direct queries on factual question-answering tasks.
Probes are substantially better calibrated than language model queries.
Most query-probe disagreements arise from confabulation (queries confident but probes uncertain) and heterogeneity (different performance on subsets), not deception.
Queries and probes are complementary, and ensembling them can improve accuracy over either alone.
The distribution of disagreement types varies across datasets, with deception being more prominent in CREAK.
papers.limitation:
Significant heterogeneity in the distribution of disagreement types across datasets, so findings may not generalize to future datasets.
Use of only a single prompt template for each experiment, which may not capture the full range of model behavior.
Only linear probes were used, and some information may be encoded non-linearly.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) can be used to evaluate the truth of factual statements in two ways: they can be either queried for statement probabilities, or probed for internal representations of truthfulness. Past work has found that these two procedures sometimes disagree, and that probes tend to be more accurate than LM outputs. This has led some researchers to conclude that LMs "lie" or otherwise encode non-cooperative communicative intents. Is this an accurate description of today's LMs, or can query-probe disagreement arise in other ways? We identify three different classes of disagreement, which we term confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity. In many cases, the superiority of probes is simply attributable to better calibration on uncertain answers rather than a greater fraction of correct, high-confidence answers. In some cases, queries and probes perform better on different subsets of inputs, and accuracy can further be improved by ensembling the two. Code is available at github.com/lingo-mit/lm-truthfulness.

papers.title: Analyze Feature Flow to Enhance Interpretation and Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do features discovered by sparse autoencoders evolve across consecutive layers of large language models, and how can this understanding be used for interpretability and model steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a data-free cosine similarity method to map Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features across transformer layers, creating flow graphs that reveal feature evolution and enable precise model steering through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-layer feature mapping framework provides granular interpretability of feature evolution in LLMs and offers a new, transparent method for steering model behavior through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Cosine similarity between SAE decoder weights effectively identifies feature relationships across layers, validated against activation correlations.
Feature formation follows distinct patterns: early layers show high entropy and feature birth, middle layers stabilize, and later layers primarily propagate existing features.
Deactivating predecessor features identified by the top-1 cosine match is causally effective, outperforming random selection.
Multi-layer steering using flow graphs is more effective and less sensitive to hyperparameters than single-layer interventions.
Flow graphs provide mechanistic insights, revealing how semantic meaning (e.g., 'particle physics') evolves and transforms across the model's computational pathway.
papers.limitation: The current steering procedure operates locally on hidden states and may not fully redirect the model's computational trajectory to a different 'minima' for truly efficient deactivation or activation.
future_direction: Further research on flow graphs as a unit of study for model interpretability.
Extending the steering experiments and flow graph analysis to other model architectures like Llama Scope.
Investigating the method's applicability and performance across a wider range of models and SAE training configurations.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new approach to systematically map features discovered by sparse autoencoder across consecutive layers of large language models, extending earlier work that examined inter-layer feature links. By using a data-free cosine similarity technique, we trace how specific features persist, transform, or first appear at each stage. This method yields granular flow graphs of feature evolution, enabling fine-grained interpretability and mechanistic insights into model computations. Crucially, we demonstrate how these cross-layer feature maps facilitate direct steering of model behavior by amplifying or suppressing chosen features, achieving targeted thematic control in text generation. Together, our findings highlight the utility of a causal, cross-layer interpretability framework that not only clarifies how features develop through forward passes but also provides new means for transparent manipulation of large language models.

papers.title: Exploration and adaptation of large language models for specialized domains
papers.research_question: Can large language models overcome challenges in specialized domains, and how can they be effectively adapted to domain-specific requirements?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation provides insights into the inner workings of LLMs and proposes adaptation methods that demonstrate LLMs can be effectively used in specialized domains, particularly clinical NLP.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models and multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.
papers.key_findings:
Layers of Transformer-based LLMs encode different dimensions of input text, with contextual representations and general language knowledge being beneficial for complex tasks.
Pre-trained language models outperform traditional approaches on clinical tasks.
Integration of domain-specific resources (like ICD hierarchy) improves model generalization.
Behavioral testing framework can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts.
Prototypical networks can provide interpretable diagnosis predictions.
papers.limitation: There is no ground truth in clinical data
future_direction: Integration of multimodal and multilingual data
Efficient methods for large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed the field of natural language processing (NLP). Their improved performance on various NLP benchmarks makes them a promising tool—also for the application in specialized domains. Such domains are characterized by highly trained professionals with particular domain expertise. Since these experts are rare, improving the efficiency of their work with automated systems is especially desirable. However, domain-specific text resources hold various challenges for NLP systems. These challenges include distinct language, noisy and scarce data, and a high level of variation. Further, specialized domains present an increased need for transparent systems since they are often applied in high stakes settings. In this dissertation, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can overcome some of these challenges and propose methods to effectively adapt them to domain-specific requirements. We first investigate the inner workings and abilities of LLMs and show how they can fill the gaps that are present in previous NLP algorithms for specialized domains. To this end, we explore the sources of errors produced by earlier systems to identify which of them can be addressed by using LLMs. Following this, we take a closer look at how information is processed within Transformer-based LLMs to better understand their capabilities. We find that their layers encode different dimensions of the input text. Here, the contextual vector representation, and the general language knowledge learned during pre-training are especially beneficial for solving complex and multi-step tasks common in specialized domains. Following this exploration, we propose solutions for further adapting LLMs to the requirements of domain-specific tasks. We focus on the clinical domain, which incorporates many typical challenges found in specialized domains. We show how to improve generalization by integrating different domain-specific resources into our models. We further analyze the behavior of the produced models and propose a behavioral testing framework that can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts. Finally, we present an approach for incorporating the benefits of LLMs while fulfilling requirements such as interpretability and modularity. The presented solutions show improvements in performance on benchmark datasets and in manually conducted analyses with medical professionals. Our work provides both new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models as well as multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.

papers.title: Using attribution to decode binding mechanism in neural network models for chemistry
papers.research_question: Why do virtual screening models make the predictions they do? The paper aims to assess the influence of dataset biases on the prediction of protein binding.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that uses attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) to test hypotheses about binding logic and reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, showing that models can achieve perfect accuracy while learning spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods can reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, and models can be fooled by adversarial examples despite perfect accuracy. Practitioners should analyze model predictions and not rely solely on aggregate accuracy metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on synthetic binding logics achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test sets but often have low attribution-AUC, indicating they learn spurious correlations.
Attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) can be used to identify dataset biases and construct adversarial examples that fool the model.
The attribution-AUC metric quantifies how well the model's attributions align with the hypothesized binding logic.
In the ADRB2 dataset, the model achieves perfect accuracy but very low attribution-AUC, indicating it does not learn the correct binding logic.
The framework provides a test for dataset bias given a hypothesis, indicating when models must be simplified/regularized or datasets augmented.
papers.limitation: Attributions offer a reductive view of the model's internal logic and fail to capture higher-order feature interactions.
future_direction: Further research to reveal feature interactions in the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy at classifying molecules with respect to whether they bind to specific protein targets. A key breakthrough would occur if these models could reveal the fragment pharmacophores that are causally involved in binding. Extracting chemical details of binding from the networks could enable scientific discoveries about the mechanisms of drug actions. However, doing so requires shining light into the black box that is the trained neural network model, a task that has proved difficult across many domains. Here we show how the binding mechanism learned by deep neural network models can be interrogated, using a recently described attribution method. We first work with carefully constructed synthetic datasets, in which the molecular features responsible for "binding" are fully known. We find that networks that achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test datasets still learn spurious correlations, and we are able to exploit this nonrobustness to construct adversarial examples that fool the model. This makes these models unreliable for accurately revealing information about the mechanisms of protein-ligand binding. In light of our findings, we prescribe a test that checks whether a hypothesized mechanism can be learned. If the test fails, it indicates that the model must be simplified or regularized and/or that the training dataset requires augmentation.

papers.title: Comparing Bottom-Up and Top-Down Steering Approaches on In-Context Learning Tasks
papers.research_question: What is the comparative effectiveness of bottom-up (function vectors) and top-down (in-context vectors) steering approaches on diverse in-context learning tasks, and under what conditions does each method excel?
papers.core_contribution: Bottom-up function vectors excel at precise functional tasks but struggle with behavioral shifts, while top-down in-context vectors are effective for behavioral shifts but less reliable for precise tasks, highlighting complementary strengths and limitations of the two steering approaches.
papers.conclusion: Both bottom-up and top-down steering methods are effective only on specific types of in-context learning tasks and cannot fully replace in-context learning, highlighting the need for a unified evaluation benchmark and better understanding of in-context learning mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Function vectors (FVs) outperform in-context vectors (ICVs) on all functional tasks (antonym, capitalize, country-capital, synonym) across zero-shot, few-shot, and natural text settings.
In-context vectors (ICVs) outperform function vectors (FVs) on behavioral tasks (detoxification, sentiment transfer), but with high variance and sensitivity to demonstration data.
ICVs are prone to causing fluency degradation and are less robust when applied in different contexts, while FVs generalize better to out-of-distribution settings.
FV performance is strongly correlated with the causal indirect effect (CIE) of attention heads, indicating that FVs rely on the existence of attention heads that significantly affect task performance.
Both steering methods have significant limitations and cannot serve as a general substitute for in-context learning, emphasizing the need for a unified evaluation benchmark.
papers.limitation:
The study only compares FVs and ICVs on a relatively small set of functional and behavioral tasks, so results may not generalize to an expanded set of tasks.
The work only considers two steering methods, so findings may not generalize to all bottom-up or top-down approaches for vector steering or interpretability.
future_direction: Expanding the scope of the study to other tasks, models, and steering methods.
Developing explanations for the variable performance of FVs and ICVs to improve understanding of in-context learning in LLMs.
papers.abstract: A key objective of interpretability research on large language models (LLMs) is to develop methods for robustly steering models toward desired behaviors. To this end, two distinct approaches to interpretability -- ``bottom-up" and ``top-down" -- have been presented, but there has been little quantitative comparison between them. We present a case study comparing the effectiveness of representative vector steering methods from each branch: function vectors (FV; arXiv:2310.15213), as a bottom-up method, and in-context vectors (ICV; arXiv:2311.06668) as a top-down method. While both aim to capture compact representations of broad in-context learning tasks, we find they are effective only on specific types of tasks: ICVs outperform FVs in behavioral shifting, whereas FVs excel in tasks requiring more precision. We discuss the implications for future evaluations of steering methods and for further research into top-down and bottom-up steering given these findings.

papers.title: Revisiting In-context Learning Inference Circuit in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the inference circuit that explains the observed phenomena of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a comprehensive 3-step inference circuit (input text encode, semantics merge, feature retrieval and copy) to characterize the inference dynamics of in-context learning in large language models, and provides empirical evidence that it captures many observed ICL phenomena and is a dominant mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed 3-step inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during in-context learning, providing a comprehensive and practical explanation of ICL inference in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models encode input text into linear, task-relevant representations in the hidden states of forerunner tokens, and this encoding is enhanced by demonstrations.
Forerunner token heads copy text representations into label tokens without selectivity, forming joint representations of label semantics and text features.
Induction heads retrieve label representations similar to the query in task-specific subspaces and copy them to the query, enabling ICL prediction.
The proposed circuit explains phenomena such as positional bias, noise robustness, and demonstration saturation in ICL.
Ablation analysis shows the circuit is a dominant mechanism for ICL, but bypass mechanisms exist in parallel.
papers.limitation: The proposed circuit may not generalize to in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios, where the query's ground-truth label is not present in the demonstrations.
future_direction: Exploring different inference dynamics in in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) is an emerging few-shot learning paradigm on Language Models (LMs) with inner mechanisms un-explored. There are already existing works describing the inner processing of ICL, while they struggle to capture all the inference phenomena in large language models. Therefore, this paper proposes a comprehensive circuit to model the inference dynamics and try to explain the observed phenomena of ICL. In detail, we divide ICL inference into 3 major operations: (1) Input Text Encode: LMs encode every input text (in the demonstrations and queries) into linear representation in the hidden states with sufficient information to solve ICL tasks. (2) Semantics Merge: LMs merge the encoded representations of demonstrations with their corresponding label tokens to produce joint representations of labels and demonstrations. (3) Feature Retrieval and Copy: LMs search the joint representations of demonstrations similar to the query representation on a task subspace, and copy the searched representations into the query. Then, language model heads capture these copied label representations to a certain extent and decode them into predicted labels. Through careful measurements, the proposed inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during the ICL process, making it a comprehensive and practical explanation of the ICL inference process. Moreover, ablation analysis by disabling the proposed steps seriously damages the ICL performance, suggesting the proposed inference circuit is a dominating mechanism. Additionally, we confirm and list some bypass mechanisms that solve ICL tasks in parallel with the proposed circuit.

papers.title: Ability Transfer and Recovery via Modularized Parameters Localization
papers.research_question: How are abilities distributed within LLM parameters? The paper investigates this by analyzing module activations under domain- and language-specific inputs for closely related models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ACT, a method that localizes ability-relevant channels in LLMs via cross-model activation differences and selectively transfers only the corresponding parameters, enabling efficient ability transfer and recovery while minimizing interference.
papers.conclusion: ACT enables efficient and effective ability transfer and recovery by localizing and transferring modularized ability-relevant parameters, and it can integrate multiple abilities into a single model with minimal interference.
papers.key_findings:
Large activation differences are concentrated in a small fraction of channels (typically <5%).
Activation difference distributions across different layers exhibit consistent heavy-tailed patterns.
Ability-specific channels are naturally disentangled across different language-domain abilities.
Ability-specific channels exhibit consistency after fine-tuning across different fine-tuned variants.
Ability-specific channels selected by activations differ from largely updated ones during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes the availability of a base model and an ability model that share the same architecture and tokenizer, and are preferably derived from the same pretrained checkpoint.
The effectiveness of ACT may be limited when the parameter drift between the base and ability models is too large, as observed in some continuous pre-training scenarios.
future_direction: Extending ACT to more diverse abilities and tasks beyond reasoning domains.
Exploring the theoretical foundations of activation-based ability localization.
Applying ACT to other model families and architectures beyond transformers.
papers.abstract: Large language models can be continually pre-trained or fine-tuned to improve performance in specific domains, languages, or skills, but this specialization often degrades other capabilities and may cause catastrophic forgetting. We investigate how abilities are distributed within LLM parameters by analyzing module activations under domain- and language-specific inputs for closely related models. Across layers and modules, we find that ability-related activations are highly concentrated in a small set of channels (typically <5\%), and these channels are largely disentangled with good sufficiency and stability. Building on these observations, we propose ACT (Activation-Guided Channel-wise Ability Transfer), which localizes ability-relevant channels via activation differences and selectively transfers only the corresponding parameters, followed by lightweight fine-tuning for compatibility. Experiments on multilingual mathematical and scientific reasoning show that ACT can recover forgotten abilities while preserving retained skills. It can also merge multiple specialized models to integrate several abilities into a single model with minimal interference. Our code and data will be publicly released.

papers.title: Beyond Interpretability: The Gains of Feature Monosemanticity on Model Robustness
papers.research_question: Does feature monosemanticity, which improves interpretability, also improve model robustness, challenging the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff?
papers.core_contribution: This paper challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff by showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also provide concrete gains in model robustness across various scenarios including noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that monosemanticity offers advantages beyond interpretability, improving model robustness across multiple learning scenarios, and advocates for exploring its broader learning benefits.
papers.key_findings:
Monosemantic features (from NCL or SAE) are more robust than polysemantic features under linear probing with label noise and input noise.
Maintaining monosemanticity during finetuning (via non-negative tuning) reduces overfitting and improves performance in few-shot and noisy-label settings.
MonoLoRA, a sparse variant of LoRA, better preserves alignment safety while maintaining task performance when finetuning LLMs on small datasets.
Empirical analysis shows that classifiers with higher robustness under noise rely more on monosemantic features.
Theoretical analysis on a toy model indicates monosemantic features have better linear separability under noise, leading to more robust decision boundaries.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from a lack of interpretability due to polysemanticity, where individual neurons are activated by multiple unrelated semantics, resulting in unclear attributions of model behavior. Recent advances in monosemanticity, where neurons correspond to consistent and distinct semantics, have significantly improved interpretability but are commonly believed to compromise accuracy. In this work, we challenge the prevailing belief of the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff, showing that monosemantic features not only enhance interpretability but also bring concrete gains in model performance. Across multiple robust learning scenarios-including input and label noise, few-shot learning, and out-of-domain generalization-our results show that models leveraging monosemantic features significantly outperform those relying on polysemantic features. Furthermore, we provide empirical and theoretical understandings on the robustness gains of feature monosemanticity. Our preliminary analysis suggests that monosemanticity, by promoting better separation of feature representations, leads to more robust decision boundaries. This diverse evidence highlights the generality of monosemanticity in improving model robustness. As a first step in this new direction, we embark on exploring the learning benefits of monosemanticity beyond interpretability, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of linking interpretability and robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/PKU-ML/Beyond_Interpretability}.

papers.title: Interpretable Pre-Trained Transformers for Heart Time-Series Data
papers.research_question: Can decoder-only transformers be effectively applied to physiological time-series data (PPG and ECG) to create interpretable pre-trained models that are easily fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as classification of heart conditions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces two interpretable pre-trained transformer models (PPG-PT and ECG-PT) for heart time-series data, demonstrating that they can be effectively fine-tuned for tasks like atrial fibrillation classification and beat detection, while providing interpretability through attention maps and embedding analysis.
papers.conclusion: This work has conclusively demonstrated that GPT-like models, trained to predict the next token in periodic physiological time series, are fully interpretable in their operation, and this interpretability is maintained when fine-tuning for classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The models' attention mechanisms focus on similar points in previous cardiac cycles and broaden their focus in deeper layers.
Tokens with the same value but occurring at different phases form separate clusters in embedding space as they propagate through the transformer.
Individual attention heads respond to specific physiologically relevant features (e.g., dicrotic notch in PPG, P-wave in ECG).
The pre-trained models can be fine-tuned quickly (11 minutes) for atrial fibrillation classification, achieving high AUC (0.99 for ECG, 0.93 for PPG).
The fine-tuned beat detector achieves a state-of-the-art F1 score of 98% and provides beat confidence values that act as a signal quality estimator.
papers.limitation: The models are pre-trained on clinical data and may not transfer well to wearable sensor data without further training.
papers.abstract: Decoder-only transformers are the backbone of the popular generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) series of large language models. In this work, we employ this framework to the analysis of clinical heart time-series data, to create two pre-trained general purpose cardiac models, termed PPG-PT and ECG-PT. We place a special emphasis on making both such pre-trained models fully interpretable. This is achieved firstly through aggregate attention maps which show that, in order to make predictions, the model focuses on similar points in previous cardiac cycles and gradually broadens its attention in deeper layers. Next, we show that tokens with the same value, which occur at different distinct points in the electrocardiography (ECG) and photoplethysmography (PPG) cycle, form separate clusters in high dimensional space. The clusters form according to phase, as the tokens propagate through the transformer blocks. Finally, we highlight that individual attention heads respond to specific physiologically relevent features, such as the dicrotic notch in PPG and the P-wave in ECG. It is also demonstrated that these pre-trained models are straightforward to fine-tune for tasks such as classification of atrial fibrillation (AF), and beat detection in photoplethysmography. For the example of AF, the fine-tuning took 11 minutes of computer time, and achieved the respective leave-one-subject-out AUCs of 0.99 and 0.93 for ECG and PPG within the MIMIC Perform AF dataset. In addition, the fine-tuned beat detector achieved a state-of-the-art F1 score of 98%, as well as uniquely providing a beat confidence level which acts as a signal quality estimator. Importantly, the fine-tuned models for AF screening are also fully explainable, with attention shifting to regions in the context that are strongly indicative of atrial fibrillation.

papers.title: Teach Old SAEs New Domain Tricks with Boosting
papers.research_question: How can we address feature blindness in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for domain-specific interpretability without requiring complete retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE Boost, a residual learning approach that trains a secondary SAE to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, enabling selective enhancement of interpretability for specialized domains without full retraining.
papers.conclusion: SAE Boost addresses feature blindness in SAEs, enabling selective domain enhancement without modifying the base model, and represents an important step forward in targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Boost significantly improves explained variance and LLM cross-entropy on domain-specific texts compared to a pretrained SAE alone.
The method maintains general domain performance with minimal degradation, confirming it learns complementary features.
SAE Boost captures domain-specific features that general-purpose SAEs miss, as shown by interpretability analysis and lower cosine similarity to base features.
The approach is modular, allowing multiple domain-specific residual SAEs to be applied simultaneously without compromising performance.
SAE Boost outperforms alternative domain adaptation methods like Extended SAE and SAE Stitching in balancing domain performance, general performance, and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Undertraining the residual SAE (e.g., on fewer than 100M tokens) can degrade general domain performance by up to 31% in explained variance.
Early stopping based solely on domain-specific metrics may lead to suboptimal feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders have emerged as powerful tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models, yet they often fail to capture domain-specific features not prevalent in their training corpora. This paper introduces a residual learning approach that addresses this feature blindness without requiring complete retraining. We propose training a secondary SAE specifically to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, effectively capturing features missed by the primary model. By summing the outputs of both models during inference, we demonstrate significant improvements in both LLM cross-entropy and explained variance metrics across multiple specialized domains. Our experiments show that this method efficiently incorporates new domain knowledge into existing SAEs while maintaining their performance on general tasks. This approach enables researchers to selectively enhance SAE interpretability for specific domains of interest, opening new possibilities for targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Understanding the patterns that neural networks learn from chemical spectra
papers.research_question: How does a neural network learn to classify infrared spectra of small organic molecules by functional groups, and what specific patterns (both intuitive and non-intuitive) does it use for classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a simpler 1D CNN that achieves state-of-the-art performance for functional group classification in infrared spectra and introduces a two-step explainability approach, revealing the network uses both characteristic group frequencies and non-intuitive patterns like tails and overtones.
papers.conclusion: The simplified CNN model is effective for spectral classification, and the explainability approach reveals the network uses both intuitive and non-intuitive spectral patterns, which can help assess generalization and guide future model design incorporating physics-based knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The 1D CNN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models while being significantly less complex.
The model consistently attends to the same spectral regions across different random initializations, indicating robust feature learning.
The network learns to use characteristic group frequencies (peaks) for classification, aligning with expert knowledge.
The network also uses non-intuitive patterns such as tails and anharmonic vibrations (overtones and combination bands) to improve classification certainty.
For some functional groups (e.g., nitriles), class imbalance and the presence of only one characteristic band lead to poor classification accuracy, highlighting dataset limitations.
papers.limitation:
Class imbalance leads to poor classification accuracy for rare functional groups like nitriles.
The network sometimes uses non-characteristic vibrations (e.g., C-H wags for halides) which may not generalize to new datasets.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based intuition into model design, e.g., using IR tables to initialize parameters or filters that optimally recognize peaks.
Transfer understanding from pretrained models to new datasets (potentially from different spectral regions).
papers.abstract: We train a convolutional neural network to classify functional groups from infrared spectra. With explainability methods, we show the model uses the presence and absence of peaks, at fundamental and anharmonic frequencies for accurate classification.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: See What You Are Told: Visual Attention Sink in Large Multimodal Models
papers.research_question: What causes the visual attention sink phenomenon in large multimodal models, and how can attention be redistributed from sink tokens to improve model performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the visual attention sink phenomenon in large multimodal models and proposes Visual Attention Redistribution (VAR), a training-free method that reallocates attention from sink tokens to non-sink visual tokens, improving model performance on various vision-language tasks.
papers.conclusion: The visual attention sink phenomenon exists in LMMs, and redistributing attention via VAR improves model performance by enhancing focus on images, offering a new perspective on understanding attention mechanisms in LMMs.
papers.key_findings:
LMMs exhibit visual attention sink, where irrelevant visual tokens receive high attention weights due to massive activation in specific hidden state dimensions.
Visual sink tokens do not contribute to model output and can be removed without performance loss.
The attention from sink tokens can be redistributed to non-sink visual tokens to enhance image focus.
VAR improves performance on general vision-language, visual hallucination, and vision-centric tasks across multiple LMMs.
VAR can be applied without additional training, models, or inference steps.
papers.limitation: Token masking experiments induce out-of-distribution behavior and have inconsistencies in random knockout across layers.
future_direction: Investigation of how visual tokens are recognized as sink tokens during training.
papers.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) "see" images by leveraging the attention mechanism between text and visual tokens in the transformer decoder. Ideally, these models should focus on key visual information relevant to the text token. However, recent findings indicate that LMMs have an extraordinary tendency to consistently allocate high attention weights to specific visual tokens, even when these tokens are irrelevant to the corresponding text. In this study, we investigate the property behind the appearance of these irrelevant visual tokens and examine their characteristics. Our findings show that this behavior arises due to the massive activation of certain hidden state dimensions, which resembles the attention sink found in language models. Hence, we refer to this phenomenon as the visual attention sink. In particular, our analysis reveals that removing the irrelevant visual sink tokens does not impact model performance, despite receiving high attention weights. Consequently, we recycle the attention to these tokens as surplus resources, redistributing the attention budget to enhance focus on the image. To achieve this, we introduce Visual Attention Redistribution (VAR), a method that redistributes attention in image-centric heads, which we identify as innately focusing on visual information. VAR can be seamlessly applied across different LMMs to improve performance on a wide range of tasks, including general vision-language tasks, visual hallucination tasks, and vision-centric tasks, all without the need for additional training, models, or inference steps. Experimental results demonstrate that VAR enables LMMs to process visual information more effectively by adjusting their internal attention mechanisms, offering a new direction to enhancing the multimodal capabilities of LMMs.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Warp: a method for neural network interpretability applied to gene expression profiles
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be interpreted in the context of gene expression analysis to recover meaningful information on a sample-specific basis?
papers.core_contribution: Warping is a method for neural network interpretability that recovers sample-specific gene signatures by interpolating in input or representation space, demonstrating effectiveness on linearly and non-linearly separable datasets.
papers.conclusion: Warping shows promise as a flexible method for post-hoc interpretation of neural networks in computational biology, enabling the examination of class gene signatures with sample-specific insights.
papers.key_findings:
Warping works well on non-linearly separable datasets like XOR, allowing data points to migrate across decision boundaries.
The method provides sample-specific bias vectors, highlighting individual adjustments needed for classification changes.
In a VAE-based approach, warping recovers biologically meaningful gene expression adjustments, such as suppressing surfactant genes and boosting kidney-specific genes to change phenotype classification.
papers.limitation:
Linear interpolation assumes the data manifold is continuous in input space, which may lead to adversarial examples.
Reconstruction blurriness caused by the variational autoencoder encoding.
future_direction: Determine how destructive warps are to other gene signatures within samples.
Overcome reconstruction blurriness caused by the VAE encoding.
papers.abstract: We show a proof of principle for warping, a method to interpret the inner working of neural networks in the context of gene expression analysis. Warping is an efficient way to gain insight to the inner workings of neural nets and make them more interpretable. We demonstrate the ability of warping to recover meaningful information for a given class on a samplespecific individual basis. We found warping works well in both linearly and nonlinearly separable datasets. These encouraging results show that warping has a potential to be the answer to neural networks interpretability in computational biology.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
